newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil offers U.S. deal over car rules.
newsitem.headline: Brazil offers U.S. deal over car rules.

text.p: Brazil has offered the United States concessions on its car industry regime that favors car manufacturers with Brazilian factories and establishes fiscal incentives for investment in Brazil's Northeast.

Brazilian and U.S. government officials who met in Rio de Janeiro to discuss U.S. complaints on the car industry rules came to no agreement on the proposals on offer but decided to hold further bilateral talks in the first half of May.

"I would describe our consultations as very productive," said Jose Alfredo Graca Lima, director of the foreign ministry's economic department. "We explained our counter proposals and the U.S. government will now evaluate these proposals.
"Sometime in the first two weeks of May our delegations will meet again to possibly reach a final agreement."

Lima said Brazil was willing to set the final date by which car manufacturers can invest in Brazil in order to benefit from the new car industry rules one year earlier than the current date of Dec. 31, 1999.

On the issue of increasing car exports to Brazil, he said, the U.S. proposal was unacceptable because it would have a negative impact on the trade balance and mean that Brazil would have to import 50 percent more cars.

"Brazil is willing to make minimal alterations," Lima said. "Brazil will allow more cars to access the Brazilian market to the extent that it will have no negative impact on the market and national industry."

Lima said Brazil's concessions on capital goods imports proposed to eliminate immediately incentives for car manufacturers to buy Brazilian-made capital goods rather than imported ones. These incentives are due to end anyway as of the beginning of next year.
Under the car industry rules, domestic manufacturers benefit from a preferential 31-percent tariff for car imports whereas manufacturers with no Brazilian production base face a stiff 62 percent tax.
The aim of the program is to spur investment in local production and exports. It has already resulted in some $20 billion in pledged investment from major global carmakers.
Brazil's other trading partners apart the United States have also protested against the car industry rules.
